The Common tailorbird Orthotomus sutorius is a small passerine widely distributed across urban and secondary growth habitats in South and Southeast Asia. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is approximately 1.05 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.05 grams], reflecting the modest energetic investment typical of small sylviid warblers. Hatchlings emerge after an incubation period of approximately 13.7 days [ab = approximately 13.7 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration consistent with the thermal constraints reported for other tropical cisticoline species.

Following hatching, nestlings exhibit a brief but intensive developmental period before achieving flight capability. The wet weight at birth is only 0.78 grams [Wwb = 0.78 grams], placing the newborn among the smallest passerine hatchlings relative to adult mass. Under the thermal conditions that prevail during the active metabolic phase of brooding adults, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging occurs just 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching]. This accelerated nestling period is an adaptive response to high nest predation risk, a selective pressure common among open-nesting birds in tropical environments. The downy chick grows rapidly on a diet of insect prey provisioned by both parents.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a predictable timeline once the individual has completed juvenile plumage development. Puberty is attained at 36 days after hatching [tp = 36 days after hatching] when ambient nesting temperatures approach 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a relatively young age compared to many temperate-zone passerines that delay reproductive onset until the following breeding season. This early gonadal maturation allows young tailorbirds to contribute to local population recruitment within their first calendar year. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 7 grams [Wwi = 7 grams] by adulthood, a body size that constrains clutch volume but supports the species' high metabolic demands during prolonged incubation bouts.

First reproduction in the Common tailorbird is deferred beyond the point of puberty, reflecting the time required to acquire a territory and secure a suitable nesting site. The time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days] when individuals are exposed to the typical active-season temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This annual breeding schedule aligns with the species' single-clutch-per-year strategy, which limits total reproductive output but may enhance offspring quality through extended parental care. Observations from a long-term study in southern India confirm that most yearling females do not lay until they have occupied a stable home range.

Maximum recorded longevity in the wild is estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years] for individuals that survive the high mortality risks of the first winter, a lifespan documented under field conditions where body temperatures during active periods average 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This comparatively long life expectancy for a bird of just 7 grams is unusual among small tropical passerines. The species' ability to persist in disturbed urban corridors may contribute to reduced predation pressure and more consistent food availability, thereby lowering extrinsic mortality. Comparative data from congeners such as Orthotomus ruficeps suggest that the tailorbird's slow life history is linked to its sedentary, territorial social system.
